items.title: Australian government bonds set for longest winning streak in more than five months
items.summary: Signs of economic weakness are fueling bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia’s next move will be a rate cut, putting Australian government bonds on track for their longest rally in more than five months. A gauge of returns is set to rise for a sixth straight session, the longest winning streak since mid-June. Australian government bonds have been among the best performers in major developed markets in 2026. They rallied sharply over the past week as a weakening labor market and November’s preliminary PMI pointed to fading growth momentum. A subdued housing market and weak consumer and business confidence have also prompted investors to bring forward rate-cut bets. “We’re starting to see some of the negative effects of rate hikes,” said Darren Langer, co-head of Australian fixed income at Yarra Capital Management. “If unemployment keeps rising at its current pace, as business surveys suggest it could, and CPI inflation eases, the RBA will consider cutting rates next year.”

items.title: BMI: South Korean consumer spending growth likely to remain modest in 2027
items.summary: BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, expects South Korean consumer spending growth to remain modest in 2027, as high inflation and sluggish nominal wage growth weigh on household purchasing power. Higher interest rates will raise debt-servicing costs for households with variable-rate mortgages and other debt. As more income goes toward debt repayment, spending on dining, leisure, apparel and household goods will weaken. High borrowing costs will also dampen big-ticket purchases, weighing on durable goods and other credit-sensitive sectors.

items.title: Huang’s reinstatement draws bipartisan scrutiny; lawmakers seek probe into possible advance trading
items.summary: After Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, lawmakers called for public testimony and a probe into the Trump administration’s role in the decision. The Senate Banking Committee’s Republican chairman said Huang will testify publicly on Dec. 3 on export controls; three House committees will question him behind closed doors next week. Democrat Elizabeth Warren called the move reckless and demanded disclosure of senior officials involved and Nvidia’s export-control compliance. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer pledged a full investigation, accusing Trump of putting personal interests ahead of national security. Democrat Ruben Gallego called for a probe into whether shares were traded before the reinstatement was announced. Republicans also questioned the national-security rationale: Senator John Cornyn challenged the claim that Huang’s return posed no risk, John Curtis sought details of government advice to the board and its basis for the decision, and Pete Ricketts said Huang must testify and Nvidia must address national-security and chip-related concerns.
